title: 3.4.21 Function Expressions and Arrow Functions
description: Eight multiple-choice questions on function values, expressions, arrow shorthand, callbacks, and hoisting. Checked instantly.

questions.question: A function named greet returns the string "Hello!". What does console.log(typeof greet) print?
options: string
Hello!
function
undefined
questions.explanation: typeof greet asks what kind of value greet is, without calling it. A function value's type is "function". "string" would be the answer to typeof greet(), because that calls the function first.

questions.question: A function greet returns "Hello!". A student writes const sayHello = greet();. What is stored in sayHello?
options: The string "Hello!" — the parentheses called the function and stored its result
The function itself, because greet is a value
A second name for greet, like const sayHello = greet;
An error, because you cannot assign a call to a const
questions.explanation: greet() calls the function immediately and yields its return value, so sayHello holds the string. Without the parentheses, const sayHello = greet; would copy the function value itself.

questions.question: Which line is a function expression rather than a function declaration?
options: function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
const add = function (a, b) { return a + b; };
function add() {}
questions.explanation: A function expression writes the function in a value position, here the right side of an assignment, and it is reached through the variable. The function itself has no name after the keyword, and the assignment ends with a semicolon.

questions.question: What does const add = (a, b) => a + b; do when you call add(2, 3)?
options: It returns undefined, because there is no return keyword
It returns 23, because the parameters are joined as text
An error, because an arrow needs the function keyword
It returns 5, because a single-expression arrow body returns that expression automatically
questions.explanation: An arrow with a single expression and no braces has an implicit return: the expression a + b is the value handed back, so add(2, 3) gives 5. No function keyword and no return keyword is required.

questions.question: What does const doubleWrong = (n) => { n * 2; }; return when you call doubleWrong(5)?
options: An error
undefined, because the braces make a block with no return
questions.explanation: Braces make the body a block, so the implicit return no longer applies. n * 2 is computed and thrown away, and with no return statement the function falls off the end and produces undefined.

questions.question: Which arrow function is written incorrectly?
options: const f = x => x + 1;
const f = (x, y) => x + y;
const f = => 42;
const f = () => 42;
questions.explanation: A function with no parameters still needs empty parentheses, so it must be const f = () => 42;. Parentheses are optional only for exactly one parameter, which is why the first option is fine.

questions.question: A helper applyTwice(operation, value) calls operation(operation(value)). Which call passes the function correctly?
options: applyTwice(double(), 5)
applyTwice(double, 5)
applyTwice(double(5), 5)
applyTwice("double", 5)
questions.explanation: A callback is passed as the function value itself, with no parentheses: applyTwice(double, 5). writing double() would call it first and hand over its result, a number, which applyTwice would then try to call and fail.

questions.question: Why does calling a function declaration on a line above its definition work, while calling a function expression above its line fails?
options: Declarations are prepared before any code runs (hoisting); an expression's variable is only filled in when its line executes
Function expressions are slower to create, so they are not ready yet
Expressions must be written with let instead of const to be hoisted
Declarations are hoisted only when called from inside another function
questions.explanation: JavaScript reads the whole file and prepares every function declaration in advance, so a declared function can be called from above. A function expression or arrow is not hoisted: its const holds nothing until execution reaches that line, so an earlier call throws a ReferenceError.
